title: Learning from a teacher
tomorrow: dying, the Buddha named no successor. so who teaches now?

segments.voice: Yesterday, finding a teacher: check first, by watching how someone lives over time. Today, once you've found one, what do you actually do?

The half-second before your hand goes up in class can feel like stepping off a ledge. Sariputta was already a serious seeker, a wanderer studying under another teacher, when he saw a monk named Assaji walking the street on his alms round. Something in the way he walked, calm, eyes lowered, unhurried, stopped Sariputta cold. If anyone has found the way, he thought, it's this one. But he didn't interrupt. He followed at a distance and waited until the alms round was done. Then he asked: who is your teacher, and what does he teach?
screen: `THE HALF-SECOND BEFORE YOUR HAND GOES UP.` → `A CALM MONK ON THE STREET.` → `WAITING, THEN ASKING.`

segments.voice: Assaji's answer is the surprise. I'm new, he says. I've only just gone forth. I can't teach it to you in detail, but I can tell you the meaning briefly. Then he gives one short verse: of the things that arise from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause, and also how they cease. That's all. A beginner, honest about being a beginner, with one line. And the Vinaya says that on hearing it, the eye of the teaching opened in Sariputta. He went straight to his friend Moggallana, who saw it in his face before he said a word, and the two of them went to the Buddha. Look at what the story keeps. A seeker who waits for the right moment instead of barging in. A question asked plainly. A teacher who says what he doesn't know. That's why asking is built into Buddhist learning: students bring questions to their teachers, lay people bring them to monks, and suttas open with questions, like the Kalamas' and Ananda's. A teacher isn't only someone who talks. A teacher is someone you ask. On Thursday, Mai has a question for the visitor.
screen: `"I'M NEW. HERE'S THE MEANING, BRIEFLY."` · `ONE VERSE: A CAUSE, AND ITS ENDING.` · `MOGGALLANA SEES IT IN HIS FACE.` · `A TEACHER IS SOMEONE YOU ASK.` · then, large: `ASK.`

segments.voice: Think of one question you've been carrying, about practice, about life, about something someone said. Say it out loud once, plainly, the way Sariputta did, as if to someone who might know. Then sit, and let it hang in the air without hurrying an answer.
Learning from a teacher: waiting for the right moment, asking plainly, and listening even when the answer is short.
Here's your line: ask, because a teacher is someone you ask. Nineteen days in, still asking.

screen: `DAY 1744 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 19 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: DYING, THE BUDDHA NAMED NO SUCCESSOR. SO WHO TEACHES NOW?`

howItsDone: Buddhists bring questions to teachers at talks, retreats and temple visits, often in a set question-and-answer time; in many monasteries a student requests an interview with a teacher to ask about their practice.

fork.setup: at a temple open day, the abbot is greeting a long line of guests. you have a real question about your meditation. what fits the Sariputta story?
options: wait till the line clears, then ask it plainly and briefly
skip it; a busy teacher's time is for students further along
ask a friend instead, since any answer is as good as his
fork.reveal: Sariputta didn't interrupt the alms round, and he didn't skip the question either. he waited for the moment, then asked plainly.

original.note: Pali: a question, the kind put to a teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: learning from a teacher means sitting through talks.
what it means: asking, at the right moment and plainly, and hearing even a short, honest answer.
what a scholar hears: in the Vinaya's account, Assaji, one of the Buddha's earliest disciples, sums up the teaching in the verse beginning ye dhamma hetuppabhava, of things arising from a cause.
guess: asking a teacher plainly, at the right moment, and listening
copying a teacher's sayings until you know them all by heart
serving a teacher for years before you're allowed to speak

chat.says: want to ask the visiting teacher something but it feels dumb and he's busy. just google it?

if it feels dumb, the answer is probably online. save him the time.
real students don't ask. they listen until the teacher brings it up.
chat.meaning: Sariputta waited until Assaji finished his alms round, then asked plainly, and one short, honest answer changed his life. Asking is how you learn from a teacher.

tie.story: Sariputta waited for Assaji to finish his alms round, then asked who his teacher was and what he taught.
tie.friend: Mai can wait for a quiet moment after Thursday's sit and ask the visiting teacher her question.
tie.you: what question have you been carrying?

Sariputta.meaning: a seeker who became one of the Buddha's chief disciples

Assaji.meaning: an early disciple whose calm walk caught Sariputta's eye

Moggallana.meaning: Sariputta's friend, who became a chief disciple too

Tathagata.meaning: a title the Buddha used for himself

alms round.meaning: a monk's walk to receive food from lay people

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.23 (Sariputta meets Assaji)

notes: Vinaya Mahavagga I.23 paraphrased: Sariputta, then a wanderer under Sanjaya, sees Assaji on alms round, is struck by his demeanor, waits until the round is finished, asks who his teacher is and what he teaches; Assaji says he is newly gone forth and can give only the meaning in brief; the verse 'ye dhamma hetuppabhava…' (of things arising from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause and their cessation) is paraphrased; the Dhamma-eye arises in Sariputta; Moggallana sees his serene face and asks; both go to the Buddha. The Vinaya says they went with Sanjaya's other followers; the count is left out on purpose. Confirm.
Gloss 'chief disciples' for Sariputta and Moggallana is standard; confirm wording.
'Suttas open with questions, like the Kalamas' and Ananda's' refers to days 1709 and 1739/1724 (AN 3.65, SN 45.2). Confirm the general statement is acceptable as phrased.
Shape: story. Mai's storyline: she wants to ask the visiting teacher at the Thursday sit a question and feels it's dumb.
Surprising fact: Assaji, who changed Sariputta's life, began by saying he was too new to teach in detail.
